title: WHY SOME CHRISTIAN MARRIAGES BECOME SEXLESS
paragraphs:
WHY SOME CHRISTIAN MARRIAGES BECOME SEXLESS
They Still Sleep in the Same Bed. They Still Say “I Love You.” They May Even Go to Church Together. But Somewhere Between the Wedding Vows and the Quiet Resentment, They Stopped Reaching for Each Other.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that almost nobody talks about in church.
It is the loneliness of lying inches away from the person you promised your life to...
and feeling miles apart.
The house may still look like a Christian home.
There may be a Bible on the nightstand.
Worship music may play in the car.
The children may see Mom and Dad sitting beside each other on Sunday.
There may still be anniversary photographs on Facebook.
There may still be “I love you” at the end of a phone call.
But when night comes...
one turns toward the wall.
The other stares into the darkness.
And neither knows how to say what has been dying between them.
Sometimes the husband feels rejected so many times that eventually he stops asking.
Sometimes the wife feels emotionally abandoned so deeply that physical intimacy begins to feel disconnected from everything her heart has been begging for.
Sometimes the roles are reversed.
Sometimes exhaustion has swallowed desire.

Sometimes childbirth, aging, grief, medication, hormonal changes, disability, chronic illness, depression, anxiety, trauma, pain, infertility, betrayal, pornography, unresolved conflict, financial pressure, caregiving, or years of accumulated disappointment have entered the bedroom with them.
Sometimes sex disappeared suddenly.
Sometimes it died one disappointed night at a time.
And sometimes two sincere Christians who genuinely love Jesus discover something frightening:
They have become excellent roommates...
but wounded lovers.
Before anyone turns this into ammunition against a spouse, hear this carefully.
This article is not permission to demand sex.
It is not permission to manipulate someone with Scripture.
It is not permission to shame a husband or wife whose body is suffering.
It is certainly not permission for coercion, intimidation, violence, or abuse.

The Bible's vision of marital intimacy cannot be separated from the Bible's commands concerning sacrificial love, honor, tenderness, faithfulness, truth, forgiveness, and concern for another person's good.
Marriage was never meant to become a courtroom where Scripture verses are presented as evidence against the person sleeping beside you.
It was meant to become a covenant in which two people increasingly learn how to love one another under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that is exactly why sexlessness can sometimes reveal something deeper than the absence of sex.
Sometimes the bedroom is where wounds from everywhere else in the marriage finally become visible.
Long before Paul wrote about marital intimacy, Scripture gave us an astonishing description of marriage.
Genesis 2:24 says that a man leaves his father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad
“One flesh.”
Not merely two people occupying one address.
Not merely two incomes paying one mortgage.
Not merely two Christians raising children under one roof.
One flesh.

Marriage is a profound covenant union, and sexual intimacy belongs within that larger reality. Sex is not the whole marriage, but neither does Scripture treat the physical union of husband and wife as meaningless.
Then Paul writes words that become uncomfortable precisely because they are so direct.

In 1 Corinthians 7:3–5, he teaches husbands and wives to give one another the marital affection that is due, and he warns them against depriving one another except temporarily by mutual agreement for prayer, after which they are to come together again.
Notice what is often missed.
Paul addresses both husband and wife.
This is not a weapon handed to husbands.
It is not a weapon handed to wives.
The passage contains a startling reciprocity. Husband and wife are called away from selfish possession and toward mutual self-giving.
And the Greek phrase connected with abstaining is deeply important:
ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou
It carries the idea of agreement, consent, being of one accord.
That matters.
Biblical marital intimacy is not supposed to look like one spouse winning while the other surrenders under pressure.
Christian marriage is not sanctified selfishness.
Sex is not a debt collector pounding on the bedroom door.
It is meant to exist within covenant love.
And perhaps that exposes one reason some Christian marriages become sexless.
Because somewhere along the journey...
intimacy stopped feeling like love.
Maybe every touch began to carry an expectation.
Maybe affection disappeared unless sex was likely.
Maybe conversations became transactional.
Maybe tenderness became rare.
Maybe one spouse started feeling that their body mattered more than their heart.
Maybe another began feeling unwanted, undesirable, and chronically rejected.
Maybe neither knew how to describe the pain without accusing the other.
So silence became safer.
Then silence became normal.
Then normal became years.
This is where Ephesians 5 becomes impossible to ignore.
Paul tells husbands:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας...
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas...
“Husbands, love your wives...”
But Paul does not stop there.
The standard is devastatingly high:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
“...as Christ loved the church.”
Think about that.
The model for a Christian husband's love is not cultural masculinity.
Not entitlement.
Not domination.
Not “I provide the money, therefore you owe me.”
Not “The Bible says your body belongs to me.”
Christ.
The crucified Christ.
The Savior who gives Himself.
The King who washes feet.
The Bridegroom who sacrifices Himself for His bride.
A husband cannot invoke 1 Corinthians 7 while conveniently forgetting Ephesians 5.
And a wife cannot use intimacy as a weapon of punishment, manipulation, contempt, or control while claiming that the rest of the marriage remains untouched.
Both husband and wife stand beneath the authority of Christ.
Both must ask the terrifying question:
“Lord, where have I stopped loving?”
Because sometimes a sexless marriage is not primarily suffering from a sex problem.
It is suffering from a tenderness problem.
A trust problem.
A forgiveness problem.
A listening problem.
A pornography problem.
A resentment problem.
A secrecy problem.
A medical problem.
A trauma problem.
An exhaustion problem.
A selfishness problem.
A communication problem.
A spiritual problem.
Or several of these at once.
And merely telling a hurting couple to “have more sex” may be like telling someone with a fractured leg to run faster.
You have not healed the fracture.
You have only increased the pain.
There is another Scripture husbands especially should sit with before blaming their wives.
Peter tells husbands to live with their wives κατὰ γνῶσιν — kata gnōsin, “according to knowledge” or with understanding, and to give them τιμήν — timēn, honor.
Then comes the sobering warning:
εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐγκόπτεσθαι τὰς προσευχὰς ὑμῶν
“So that your prayers may not be hindered.”
—1 Peter 3:7
That should stop a Christian man cold.
God cares about how you treat your wife.
Your spirituality at church cannot be neatly separated from your behavior at home.
You cannot become cruel at 8:00 p.m. and imagine that religious language at 8:00 a.m. makes cruelty disappear.
You cannot humiliate your wife, ignore her pain, treat her as an object, and then consider yourself spiritually healthy simply because you know theology.
Peter connects a husband's treatment of his wife with his prayers.
That is serious.
And wives should not read that paragraph merely thinking, “I hope my husband sees this.”
The Gospel does not merely expose the person beside us.
It exposes us.
What have I done with my spouse's vulnerability?
Have I listened?
Have I mocked?
Have I punished?
Have I compared?
Have I withdrawn affection to gain power?
Have I made confession dangerous?
Have I made rejection habitual?
Have I become harsh?
Have I become contemptuous?
Have I carried secret fantasies into our covenant?
Have I expected my spouse to heal wounds I refuse to acknowledge?
Have I prayed for my marriage while refusing to repent inside my marriage?
Those questions hurt.
They are supposed to.
Because repentance often begins where excuses end.
And this is where pornography deserves to be named.
Pornography trains desire away from covenant and toward consumption.
It teaches the eyes to demand novelty while a real spouse grows older beside you.
It offers fantasy without responsibility, bodies without covenant, stimulation without sacrifice.
Then the person consuming it may wonder why ordinary marital intimacy no longer produces the same excitement.
Jesus takes lust seriously.
In Matthew 5:28, He brings the battle into the heart.
The answer, however, is not merely shame.
It is repentance.
Bring darkness into light.
Confess.
Remove access.
Seek accountability.
Stop protecting the thing destroying your ability to see another human being with holy love.
And if pornography has wounded your marriage, do not demand that trust regenerate overnight.
Broken trust may be forgiven before it is fully rebuilt.
Forgiveness and restored trust are related, but they are not identical processes.
Trust often returns through truth consistently practiced over time.
But pornography is not the explanation for every sexless marriage.
Sometimes there is no secret scandal.
There is simply pain.
A woman may experience painful intercourse and remain silent because she thinks a “good Christian wife” is supposed to endure it.
A husband may experience sexual dysfunction and drown in shame because he believes admitting it makes him less masculine.
A new mother may be physically exhausted, touched-out, hormonally changed, and emotionally overwhelmed.
A spouse taking necessary medication may experience changes in desire or sexual functioning.
Illness can change bodies.
Menopause can change bodies.
Pregnancy can change bodies.
Grief can change bodies.
Trauma can change bodies.
Age changes bodies.
And Christian compassion must be large enough to acknowledge bodies without treating every difficulty as rebellion against God.
Sometimes the faithful next step is prayer.
Sometimes it is repentance.
Sometimes it is a difficult conversation.
Sometimes it is a physician.
Sometimes it is a qualified counselor.
Sometimes it is a trustworthy pastor working alongside appropriate professional care.
And when trauma, coercion, violence, or abuse is present, the priority is not pressuring someone into sexual availability. Safety and appropriate help matter.
There is no holiness in forcing a wounded person to pretend they are healed.
Jesus does not need your marriage to look impressive.
He wants truth.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this has been afraid of.
Truth.
Because truth might require saying:
“I don't feel close to you anymore.”
“I feel rejected.”
“I feel pressured.”
“I don't feel safe enough to be vulnerable.”
“I miss you.”
“I am ashamed of what I have been watching.”
“I am carrying resentment.”
“I have been pretending.”
“I am exhausted.”
“Something hurts.”
“I don't know why my desire disappeared.”
“I need help.”
“I was wrong.”
“Please forgive me.”
Those sentences can feel terrifying after years of avoidance.
But imagine something.
Tonight, instead of beginning with accusations, imagine sitting beside your spouse and saying:
“I don't want to fight about sex anymore. I want to understand what happened to us.”
That sentence could change the temperature of a room.
Not because it magically fixes everything.
But because curiosity is different from accusation.
“I want to understand you” is different from “You owe me.”
“I miss us” is different from “You always reject me.”
“Have I hurt you?” is different from “What is wrong with you?”
“What do you need me to understand?” is different from “Why can't you just change?”
Christian intimacy grows where truth and grace are allowed into the same room.
That is the Gospel pattern itself.
Truth does not disappear.
Sin is not renamed.
Wounds are not minimized.
But grace enters where shame expected execution.
That is what Jesus does.
Think about the scandal of the Gospel.
We were not desirable because we had perfected ourselves.
We were sinners needing mercy.
Christ did not wait for us to become spotless and then decide we were worth loving.
He moved toward sinners in redeeming love.
Romans 5:8 tells us that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
The cross exposes our sin and simultaneously announces God's astonishing grace.
That does not mean spouses become one another's saviors.
Only Jesus saves.
But it means Christian marriage has a Savior to whom two broken people can return.
Maybe your marriage has become cold.
Jesus is not cold.
Maybe trust has been damaged.
Jesus is faithful.
Maybe sin has been hidden.
Jesus already knows.
Maybe you are ashamed.
The cross was built for guilty people who finally stop hiding.
Maybe you have sinned against your spouse.
Repent.
Not performatively.
Not because you want sex tonight.
Not because you want the argument to disappear.
Repent because Christ is Lord.
Name what you did.
Stop defending it.
Ask forgiveness without demanding immediate emotional recovery from the person you wounded.
Then bear fruit consistent with repentance.
Maybe you are the wounded spouse.
Grace does not require calling evil good.
Forgiveness does not require pretending nothing happened.
Reconciliation should involve truth, repentance, wisdom, and the rebuilding of what has been damaged.
And in situations involving abuse, seek safety and qualified help rather than allowing spiritual language to pressure you into remaining exposed to harm.
But for many couples reading this, there may be no dramatic betrayal.
Just distance.
Years of it.
And perhaps tonight God is not asking you to manufacture passion.
Perhaps He is asking you to take one honest step toward the person you married.
Put down the phone.
Turn off the television.
Sit together.
Ask a question you have been avoiding.
Then listen without preparing your defense.
Maybe hold hands and pray even if the prayer is awkward.
Maybe the prayer is only:
“Jesus, we don't know how we got here. Please teach us how to love each other again.”
That is enough to begin.
Because the goal is not merely getting sex back.
The deeper goal is bringing the marriage back under the transforming lordship of Jesus Christ.
You can have frequent sex and still have a spiritually unhealthy marriage.
You can also walk through a medically or circumstantially necessary season without sex and remain deeply faithful, tender, and united.
So the question cannot simply be:
“How often are you having sex?”
The better questions are:
Are you loving?
Are you truthful?
Are you faithful?
Are you honoring one another?
Are you listening?
Are you repenting?
Are you forgiving?
Are you seeking your spouse's good?
Are you willing to get help?
Is Christ actually Lord inside your home?
Because Christian marriage was never intended merely to survive until death.
It is meant to testify that covenant love does not run away the moment love becomes costly.
And perhaps that is why this subject feels so personal.
Somebody has been crying quietly over this.
Somebody feels unwanted.
Somebody feels used.
Somebody feels ashamed.
Somebody misses the person sleeping beside them.
Somebody has stopped initiating because another rejection feels unbearable.
Somebody has stopped responding because intimacy no longer feels emotionally safe.
Somebody has been asking God to repair a marriage while secretly wondering whether anything can ever change.
If that is you, do not turn this article into another weapon.
Turn it into a doorway.
Go first.
Not necessarily by initiating sex.
By initiating truth.
Initiate tenderness.
Initiate repentance.
Initiate listening.
Initiate prayer.
Initiate the appointment with the doctor if something physical may be wrong.
Initiate counseling if the two of you keep reopening the same wounds.
Initiate accountability if secret sin is poisoning the covenant.
Initiate forgiveness where genuine repentance is present.
Initiate the conversation you keep postponing.
You may discover that what died between you was not desire first.
Maybe desire was simply one of the last things to disappear.
And perhaps what needs resurrection is not merely the bedroom...
but friendship.
Safety.
Affection.
Honor.
Trust.
Laughter.
Gentleness.
Spiritual intimacy.
The ability to be known without being punished for being vulnerable.
That kind of restoration may take time.
Do not confuse slow healing with failed healing.
God often works through ordinary obedience repeated faithfully.
A softer answer.
An honest confession.
A doctor's visit.
A counseling appointment.
A deleted account.
A boundary honored.
A promise kept.
A hand held without demanding anything afterward.
A sincere apology.
A prayer whispered in the dark.
One step.
Then another.
Then another.
Until one day two people realize they are no longer standing on opposite sides of the wound.
They are standing together before Christ.
And that is where grace becomes breathtaking.
The Gospel Warrior message has always been:
Not because every marriage receives the exact ending we imagined.
Not because consequences magically vanish.
Not because Scripture guarantees instant restoration of sexual intimacy.
But because Jesus Christ still transforms sinners.
He still brings hidden things into light.
He still teaches selfish hearts to serve.
He still gives grace to repent.
He still gives strength to forgive.
He still heals what human effort alone cannot heal.
He still takes people whose stories look hopeless and begins writing something grace could produce but pride never could.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that seeking help, repentance, patience, and grace are worth pursuing.
Not because every paragraph applies to every marriage, but because difficult conversations are rarely solved in one reading.
Some struggles deserve privacy.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedient, generous, truthful lives. But supporting Gospel-centered ministry can help truth travel farther.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the husband who has stopped hoping.
Invite the wife who feels invisible.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
Invite the seeker who still wonders whether Jesus has anything to say to broken people.
Even invite the unbeliever who believes Christianity is only for people whose lives already look perfect.
Let them discover something different.
Grace is for people who know they need rescue.
But before you leave this article and return to scrolling...
look at the person beside you differently tonight.
Not as the enemy.
Not as the obstacle standing between you and happiness.
Not merely as the person who stopped touching you.
See a human soul.
A fellow image-bearer.
Someone with fears you may not completely understand.
Someone who may also be hurting.
Someone Christ commands you to love with truth.
And perhaps the first miracle your marriage needs tonight is not passion.
Perhaps it is two wounded people finally putting down their weapons long enough to kneel before the same Savior.
Because sometimes the distance between two pillows can feel like a thousand miles...
but Jesus can begin rewriting a marriage the moment two hearts stop hiding from the truth and start surrendering to His grace.
